introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 3 (0790), Paper 3 (Critical Thinking), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing TWO questions from each section (Section One: Logic; Section Two: Philosophical Problems). Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- Coherence and organization of material;
- Clear presentation of the problematic;
- Identification and development of the Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis and Conclusion, as prescribed.

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION ONE: LOGIC**

*Read the passage below and answer the questions that follow:*

> Colonization is the worst experience Africa has ever had. If Africa is not developed today then either Africa is the cause or the colonial masters are guilty. Some African countries today are underdeveloped entities given that some African countries are victims. Either natives fought and died or they allowed their resources to be exploited. There is no doubt that some Europeans are racists; and if some are, it only proves that all of them could be racist. Thus, the future of Africa lies in her hands. While some analysts blame the west for all the problems Africa faces, others think that the African problem of the past just like today is that Africans don't read and thus are not aware of their rights and the need to fight for human equality. The future lies then in the hands of the youths, though some youths are not serious citizens

**Questions**
incertitudes: Q1(a)(ii) : « the contradictory of its subaltern » est ambigu : une proposition I est elle-même la subalterne de la A de mêmes termes. Lecture retenue : on part de la A (« All African countries today are underdeveloped entities »), liée à a(i) par subalternation, puis on prend sa contradictoire (la O). Résultat : indéterminé, quelle que soit la lecture (I vrai ne dit rien de A ni de O, I et O étant subcontraires). Vérifié avec Python (modèles d'ensembles).

Q1(a)(i) : plusieurs I-propositions dans le passage (« some African countries are underdeveloped entities », « some African countries are victims », « some Europeans are racists ») ; la première est retenue comme référence de a(ii) et a(iii), les autres sont mentionnées comme acceptables.

Q1(b)(i) : plusieurs enthymèmes sont possibles dans le passage ; celui de la phrase « Some African countries today are underdeveloped entities given that some African countries are victims » est retenu (conclusion + prémisse mineure : enthymème du premier ordre, prémisse majeure supprimée). Convention des ordres : 1er ordre = majeure omise, 2e ordre = mineure omise, 3e ordre = conclusion omise. Forme AII-1 (Darii) vérifiée valide par Python.

Q1(c)(ii)-(iii) : le modus ponendo tollens est valide pour une disjonction exclusive seulement ; la disjonction « either ... or » du passage est lue comme inclusive (v), d'où l'invalidité (contre-modèle F = E = vrai, vérifié avec Python).

Q1(d)(i) : le dilemme destructeur simple est construit avec les éléments de la phrase conditionnelle du passage (N antécédent, C et G les deux membres de l'alternative) : N ⊃ (C v G) n'est pas strictement équivalent à (N ⊃ C) · (N ⊃ G) ; la construction illustre la forme demandée (validité de la forme vérifiée avec Python), elle n'est pas une conséquence logique du passage.

Q1(e) : plusieurs sophismes sont repérables dans le passage (généralisation hâtive, faux dilemme, non sequitur) ; la généralisation hâtive est retenue comme réponse principale, les autres sont mentionnés comme acceptables.
Points : (a) 1+2+3 = 6 ; (b) 2+3 = 5 ; (c) 1+3+2 = 6 ; (d) 3+3 = 6 ; (e) 2 ; total 25, conforme aux 25 marks imprimés.

Numérotation : le sujet imprime « 3. », « 4. », « 5. », « 6. » ; les questions 1 et 2 n'ont pas de numéro lisible (la question 1 est annoncée par le passage de lecture, la question 2 par un point isolé devant « (a) »). Numéros déduits de la suite 1 à 6 ; la section Logic compte donc trois questions, la section Philosophical Problems trois.

Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « answer FOUR questions, choosing TWO questions from each section » (quatre questions au total, deux par section). Section One (Logic) : questions 1 à 3 ; Section Two (Philosophical Problems) : questions 4 à 6. `regles_choix` porte une règle `parmi 2 sur 3` par section ; la règle « 4 en tout » est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Aucun corrigé officiel : le corrigé est une réponse modèle rédigée ; la logique est recalculée avec Python (itertools, modèles d'ensembles), la philosophie est donnée de mémoire (auteurs et positions de l'histoire établie de la philosophie, sans citation littérale, titre d'ouvrage, date ni numéro de page). À faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**1.** (a) From the passage:

(i) Identify a categorical proposition with both terms undistributed. (1 mark)

(ii) Given a (i) above as true, what can be inferred of the contradictory of its subaltern? (2 marks)

(iii) Contradict the obverse a (i) above. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (1 mark).** A categorical proposition whose two terms are both undistributed is an **I-proposition** ("Some S are P"): the subject is undistributed (only some S are meant) and the predicate is undistributed (an affirmative proposition says nothing about all P). The passage contains one: **"Some African countries today are underdeveloped entities."** (S = African countries today; P = underdeveloped entities). (Also acceptable: "Some African countries are victims" and "Some Europeans are racists".)

**(ii) (2 marks).** Let a(i) be the I-proposition "Some African countries today are underdeveloped entities". Subalternation links it to the universal affirmative **A**: "All African countries today are underdeveloped entities" (the A is the superaltern, the I its subaltern). The contradictory of that A-proposition is the **O-proposition**: "Some African countries today are not underdeveloped entities."

- In the traditional square of opposition, the truth of a particular (I) gives **no information** about the universal (A): the inference from particular to universal is not allowed.
- Since the A is undetermined, its contradictory (the O) is undetermined too. The same result follows from the fact that I and O are **subcontraries**: both can be true together, so the truth of I leaves the O open.

**Conclusion:** nothing can be inferred; the contradictory is **undetermined (doubtful)**, it may be true or false.

**(iii) (3 marks).**

- Obverse of a(i): obversion changes the quality of the proposition and replaces the predicate by its complement. "Some African countries today are underdeveloped entities" becomes the **O-proposition** "Some African countries today are **not non-underdeveloped** entities."
- Contradictory of that O-proposition (the A-proposition with the same terms): **"All African countries today are non-underdeveloped entities"**, that is, "All African countries today are developed (not underdeveloped) entities."

Check: the contradictory of a(i) is the E-proposition "No African country today is an underdeveloped entity", whose obverse is exactly "All African countries today are non-underdeveloped entities": both routes give the same result.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Identify an enthymematic argument from the passage and state the Order. (2 marks)

(ii) Supply the missing proposition of b(i) and state the form of the syllogism. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (2 marks).** The sentence "Some African countries today are underdeveloped entities **given that** some African countries are victims" is an enthymeme: it states a conclusion and only one premise.

- Stated conclusion: Some African countries today are underdeveloped entities.
- Stated premise: Some African countries are victims. It contains the minor term (African countries) and the middle term (victims): it is the **minor premise**.
- Suppressed: the **major premise**, which links the middle term (victims) to the major term (underdeveloped entities).

An enthymeme whose major premise is suppressed is an enthymeme of the **first order** (second order: the minor premise is suppressed; third order: the conclusion is suppressed).

**(ii) (3 marks).** The missing proposition is the major premise: **"All victims are underdeveloped entities."** (an A-proposition). The complete syllogism is:

- Major premise (A): All victims are underdeveloped entities. ($M$ a $P$)
- Minor premise (I): Some African countries are victims. ($S$ i $M$)
- Conclusion (I): Therefore, some African countries are underdeveloped entities. ($S$ i $P$)

**Form:** the middle term (victims) is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise: this is the **first figure**. The mood is A-I-I. The syllogism is therefore of the form **AII-1 (Darii)**. It is valid: the middle term is distributed once (subject of the A-proposition), no term is distributed in the conclusion that was not distributed in its premise, and the conclusion is affirmative like both premises. (Validity does not make it sound: the premise "All victims are underdeveloped entities" is open to doubt.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Identify a disjunctive proposition from the passage. (1 mark)

(ii) Using c(i), construct a Modus Ponendo Tollens argument. (3 marks)

(iii) Why is c(ii) considered an invalid form of the disjunctive syllogism? (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (1 mark).** **"Either natives fought and died or they allowed their resources to be exploited."** Symbolised: $F \vee E$ (F: the natives fought and died; E: the natives allowed their resources to be exploited). (Another disjunction: "either Africa is the cause or the colonial masters are guilty", but it is embedded in the consequent of a conditional.)

**(ii) (3 marks).** Modus ponendo tollens (MPT) is the mode of the disjunctive syllogism that **affirms** one disjunct in the minor premise in order to **deny** the other in the conclusion: $p \vee q,\ p\ /\ \therefore\ \sim q$.

- Major premise: Either the natives fought and died or they allowed their resources to be exploited. ($F \vee E$)
- Minor premise: The natives fought and died. ($F$)
- Conclusion: Therefore, the natives did not allow their resources to be exploited. ($\therefore\ \sim E$)

**(iii) (2 marks).** MPT is valid only when the disjunction is **exclusive** ("either ... or ..., but not both"). The symbol $\vee$ stands for an **inclusive** (weak) disjunction, which is true when **both** disjuncts are true. Then affirming one disjunct does not allow us to deny the other: the argument commits the **fallacy of affirming a disjunct**.

Proof by truth table: take $F = T$ and $E = T$. Both premises are true ($F \vee E = T$ and $F = T$) while the conclusion $\sim E$ is false, so the form is invalid. In the passage this is realistic: the natives could have fought and died **and** still have seen their resources exploited. The valid mode for an inclusive disjunction is modus tollendo ponens: $p \vee q,\ \sim p\ /\ \therefore\ q$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) Identify a suitable proposition from the passage and use it to construct a simple destructive dilemma. (3 marks)

(ii) Evade the dilemma above by escaping between the horns. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (3 marks).** Suitable proposition: **"If Africa is not developed today then either Africa is the cause or the colonial masters are guilty."** Let $N$: Africa is not developed today; $C$: Africa is the cause; $G$: the colonial masters are guilty.

A **simple destructive dilemma** has two conditionals with the **same antecedent**, a disjunctive premise that **denies their consequents**, and a conclusion that denies the common antecedent:
$(p \supset q) \cdot (p \supset r),\ \sim q \vee \sim r\ /\ \therefore\ \sim p$.

- Premise 1: If Africa is not developed today, then Africa is the cause; and if Africa is not developed today, then the colonial masters are guilty. $(N \supset C) \cdot (N \supset G)$
- Premise 2: But either Africa is not the cause or the colonial masters are not guilty. $\sim C \vee \sim G$
- Conclusion: Therefore, Africa is developed today. $\therefore\ \sim N$

The form is valid (checked by truth table: no row makes the three lines true with $N$ true).

**(ii) (3 marks).** To **escape between the horns** is to show that the **disjunctive premise is false**: the alternatives it offers are not the only possibility. Here the second premise says that at least one of $C$ and $G$ is false. Escape: **both are true.** Africa can be partly the cause (poor governance, corruption, lack of education and civic engagement, as some analysts in the passage argue) **and** the colonial masters can be guilty (exploitation of resources, arbitrary borders, the undermining of local institutions, as other analysts argue). Then $\sim C \vee \sim G$ is false, the dilemma lacks a true disjunctive premise, and its conclusion that Africa is developed is not established. (The passage itself admits both explanations, which shows that responsibility is shared.)

questions.enonce_markdown: (e) Identify a fallacy from the passage and state how it is committed. (2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Fallacy: hasty generalisation** (drawing a conclusion about a whole class from a few cases).

The passage says: "There is no doubt that some Europeans are racists; and if some are, it only proves that all of them could be racist." The premise concerns **some** (an unspecified part of the) Europeans; the conclusion extends the property to **all** of them. The evidence is too small and unrepresentative to support a claim about the whole class: that some members of a group have a trait does not show that every member could have it (it is the illicit passage from an I-proposition to an A-proposition).

(Other acceptable answers: a **false dilemma**, "Either natives fought and died or they allowed their resources to be exploited", which ignores other possibilities such as resisting partly and being exploited anyway; or a **non sequitur**, "Thus, the future of Africa lies in her hands", which does not follow from the preceding sentences.)
